title: The Problem with Your New Years Resolution
author: Arthur Brooks
source: The Free Press (The Pursuit of Happiness with Arthur Brooks), January 12, 2026
summary: Brooks argues that most failed New Year's resolutions don't reflect a character flaw — they reflect a lousy resolution. Drawing on data that 22 percent of resolution-makers have failed by week one, 50 percent by three months, and 81 percent after two years, he reframes the problem from willpower to design: resolutions are good (they're a sign you want to improve your life in tangible ways, which is healthy and positive) but the smartness of the design determines whether they survive. The article opens with Brooks' personal story of quitting smoking at 26, when he fell asleep with a lit cigarette and woke to ten holes burned in his sheets while engaged to be married — an event that converted an abstract concern (smoking will eventually kill me) into a concrete trigger (it might kill the future Mrs. Brooks). The piece treats people as needing 'something in their lives that's worth striving for' and the rest of the essay (largely behind The Free Press paywall) lays out how to design resolutions that survive the compounding failure rates. Note: the inline email text is partial; the full essay sits at thefp.com behind subscription, but the core thesis (resolutions are valuable; design determines survival; concrete triggers beat abstract goals) is fully visible.
points: Most failed resolutions aren't evidence of a character flaw; they're evidence of bad resolution design — 22 percent fail by week one, 50 percent by three months, 81 percent after two years.
Resolutions themselves are valuable: they signal that someone wants to improve life in tangible ways and treat striving as a healthy human need, not a self-help indulgence.
Concrete triggers (Brooks' lit cigarette burning ten holes in sheets while engaged to be married) convert abstract concerns into action in a way that abstract intentions ('I should quit') do not.
The piece reframes the problem from willpower to design — the right question is how to make a resolution that doesn't break, not whether you have the discipline to honour a brittle one.
People need something in their lives that's worth striving for; the answer to high failure rates is smarter resolutions, not abandoning resolutions.
quotes: It's the second week of 2026. Have you kept your New Year's resolution? For many, the answer is probably no. Perhaps you are reading this sentence while, filled with self-loathing, you eat something you vowed to forgo in 2026.
Of about half of all Americans who make New Year's resolutions on January 1, 22 percent have failed at the end of week one; 50 percent at three months; and 81 percent after two years.

Knowing this, you might conclude that New Year's resolutions are stupid. That would be a mistake. Resolutions are very good, in fact: They are a sign that you want to improve your life in tangible ways, which is healthy and positive. People need something in their lives that's worth striving for.

I used to wake up each night around 3 a.m. and light up a coffin nail right there in the bed. But one night at age 26, when I was engaged to be married, I fell back asleep with a lit cigarette, and woke up later with 10 holes burned in the sheets.
It occurred to me that it was one thing for the cigs to kill me, but quite another for them to kill the future Mrs. Brooks.
You just have to be smart about how to make your resolutions.” Archived from The Free Press (The Pursuit of Happiness with Arthur Brooks) on May 1, 2026 by Tim.
